replies.author: Spudly42
replies.body:
Yeah you do need to have some task management architecture to do it without conflicting, but essentially each editor has it's own workspace so there isn't much clashing unless your task queueing didn't know two things would touch the same files.  You can generally avoid this with some grooming step, though.

I run 2 instances on one machine and the most useful part is being able to run coop tasks where you can test your multiplayer is working as expected.  You definitely would need a lot of RAM to run more than 2 and the other thing is if your trying to do any performance evaluation stuff, it's going to mess with your numbers obviously if you have another editor in play mode.  Overall it works pretty well, but yeah once you get to this level if you have your task drain systems running overnight on multiple lanes, you will burn through more than 1 full Claude subscription in a few days and you yourself will also become a bottleneck.

replies.author: Kompicek
replies.body:
Yeah UE is horrible with concurrent edits, I dont recommend using them. Basically try to focus on the process more as a company with many people would. Lets say that you want to develop a new feature. You first need a designer\\architect that does proper research and prepares implementation plan that is split into areas that can be built separately. This is reviewed by another agent, because it is crucial. Once it is approved it gets sent automatically to project manager who leads the development, he knows his team well and splits tasks appropriately.  Each agent does his individual work end to end including tests. After that it goes to auditors which merge the work, one piece at a time or return it back for adjustment. They check the whole project architecture so even if you dont have conflicts they may refuse the work and give it back to project manager. I am describing only part of the process not the whole end to end workflow.

On the unreal part, every agent has its own worktree and its own copy of the project on its own branch. Most of the time agents are only writing c++ like in normal IDE and open editors only for tests and compiling ( which can also be shared with UBA cache so you dont compile 100x the same over and over). In terms of assets you need to be way more careful and have only one owner at a time otherwise agents may and will step on each others feet.

Splitting everything into individual plugins is in my opinion unrealistic for every feature. Also please note that it is not only unreal when you are making a game, you have blender, you have marvelous designer, comfyui, external tools via API, you have multiple individual labs for testing combat\\physics\\clothing etc.

Sorry for the long wall of text and sorry for my English. It is a bit hard for me to explain something like this not in my native language :)

replies.author: lazy_lockstep
replies.body:
The same reason you would want multiple employees in a company.

If each agent is an "employee", then it needs its own execution environment for testing.

The more resources each agent can access, the more productive it can be.

The bottleneck in that scenario would be merging all the conflicting code at the end, and/or planning for parallelization at the beginning.

With limited Editor resources, you've added another bottleneck: Access to the editor. It can be worked around simply enough, by making the editor a shared, limited resource, with 'slots', schedules, pipelines, or some other allocation mechanism. But, all things being equal: an organization that doesn't need to add the overhead to accommodate an arbitrary limitation will be faster/more efficient.  

Having said that: The agents working on my current game's repo's don't seem to be using the Editor directly any more. I started them down the path of a 'slot' system with a 6 slot max. The editor itself doesn't load any more, which... fair enough. It's not like they need to interact with the GUI elements directly.
